Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Jeremy TeGrotenhuis
Email: 
General Comment
As both an educator and a creative writer, I urge the AI action plan of the United States needs to restrain the abusive and rights-violating
practices of AI developers and institute guard-rails to prevent AI tools from depriving the next generation of the opportunity to learn skills
and develop their intellect.
That last point is important, so I will start there. As a teacher, I have seen how destructive large language models are to the education
system. It has always been the case that many students would rather not do the work required to learn. Now, there is a perfect tool for
them to avoid work, one that can generate the kinds of simple essays or complete the kinds of simple math problems or lab reports that
students are assigned (and even include some of the simple mistakes that students tend to make - more on that later!). American education
is already struggling. Generative AI has only made that struggle worse, as students turn to and educators are forced to take time away
from actually teaching, giving feedback, or developing lessons to identify and document this AI-plagiarism.
Some large language models and AI tools have their uses, particularly in the sciences and medical fields. Generative AI, however, is
largely a scam. This technology is impressive to the ignorant, but embarrassing to the informed. It makes frequent mistakes, provides
factually inaccurate responses to prompts, and will invent sources of information whole-sale. Notoriously, lawyers have been reprimanded
and sanctioned by the courts for utilizing AI that fabricated case law that did not actually exist. Researchers have been caught submitting
bibliographies that include citations to papers which were never published. These tools present themselves as reliable, but they do not
process information or knowledge. They simply produce strings of text or tokens based on a complex statistical process, guessing what
should come next to satisfy the person who queried them. Referring to these tools as "intelligent" is largely a marketing ploy. They are not
meaningfully so, and some researchers have openly stated skepticism about their ability to ever become so. Why should we then obliterate
our copyright system, which protects the ability of working creatives to make a living, in order to facilitate the further development of these
massively expensive, resource-devouring machines that do not even do the thing they claim to do?
Sam Altman has publicly admitted that AI development is impossible without stealing from creatives. That the need of these models for
training data is so enormous and insatiable that the copyright system must be done away with to feed them. To that I say, if you cannot
operate your business in a way that is fair and legal, you do not have the right to operate your business. And the fact that Altman's
businesses are massively unprofitable and require constant injections of venture capital, even as his company has blatantly stolen data and
creative work to feed their machines, reveals that even WHILE breaking the law he cannot create something worthwhile.
At the end of the day, these AI-boosters believe that this product is worth developing for the simple reason that it will one day replace
workers. That they will no longer need to pay skilled American trades and craftspeople to develop software, write prose, create art, or,
eventually, do any other work at all. They dream of a world without us, where our work has been used to feed a general artificial
intelligence which they can then use to replace us. And to build it, they want to steal from us. They want to take our work, and then
enslave us by proxy through the machine they will build with our work. It is a travesty of justice and a betrayal of the American people to
allow this to happen.

Why should we then obliterate our copyright system... to facilitate the further development of these massively expensive, resource-devouring machines... At the end of the day, these AI-boosters believe that this product is worth developing for the simple reason that it will one day replace workers.
AI-RFI-2025-6163.rationale: The commenter explicitly calls for “guard-rails” and restraining “rights-violating practices,” indicating stronger oversight. They also argue against weakening copyright protections for training data and describe harms to education and potential worker replacement, plus broader consumer/rights harms.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Anonymous Anonymous
General Comment
From:
Noah B. Swiatek
3D Animator
Rancho Cucamonga, California
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

General Comment
AI ACTION PLAN
Sir:
the recent work of the organization Open AI, as communicated to the world through the release of ChatGPT, leads me to believe that
both current and potential developments in artificial intelligence call for watchfulness and, indeed, quick action on the part of your
administration. 
We find ourselves in a situation not wholly dissimilar to that prior to the Manhattan Project, where the potential to develop a powerful new
type of bomb existed for the Allies and for Germany. Today a global race for expanded AI capabilities has begun without adequate
governmental oversight. Beyond this, any future advantages in AI by China or other adversaries that would alter the balance of power
militarily or in other spheres must not be allowed to happen. 
As FDR did with the Manhattan Project, you may find it desirable to put in place an organization under direct government control which is
empowered to bring together the resources and talent needed to accelerate developments in AI and coordinate with other organizations.
No one knows what future progress in AI may occur, how quickly, and how it may impact American national interests. What is clear is
that potential for the development of future powerful AI technology exists and must not be left solely in the hands of non-governmental
organizations and corporations.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I love art. I love books and the written word. I love paint and colored pencils and digital renderings. I love songs and photographs,
television shows and movies. Even clothes are an art form and I love them and the truly infinite ways art and creativity influence my life.
Unfortunately, the AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of
American artists, songwriters, authors, and even small businesses with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. The unique works of hundreds of thousands of other
everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without consent or compensation. They ingest the work, reassemble
it, and then sell it back to the public. This is direct competition for those artists who created the work in the first place and completely cuts
them out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How can people possibly make a
living doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that they can decide when and where
their work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Their work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

A letter on the Harmful use of AI and Copyright

March 14, 2025 
From: 
CHRISTOPHER ONDRACEK 
SELF EMPLOYED FREELANCE ARTIST 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who works to provide artistic skills to clients of all manners. I have 
worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been 
lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
●
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.
●
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original
creators, not just Big Tech.
●
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies,
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what
content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technologyI. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of 
Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law. Those who steal the years of 
labor, training, and expertise of others to benefit from it and claim it to be their own should not 
be allowed to make the decision for the ones they steal from.​
We are artists who are being threatened day by day in the current state of this world. Protect the 
artists. Protect the future of creativity. This country is meant to be built on the ideals of freedom, 
and artists should have the freedom to create without worry of their life’s work being stolen for 
the pockets of the greedy corporations looking to eradicate that creativity. 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

AI Salon Response to WH AI RFI

March 15, 2025 
Faisal D'Souza  
National Coordinator Office  
Networking and Information Technology Research and Development Program 
National Science Foundation 
2415 Eisenhower Avenue 
Alexandria, VA 22314 
RE: Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) 
Action Plan 
Dear Mr. D’Souza, 
On behalf of the AI Salon (the Salon), a community of more than 3,000 AI optimists 
collaboratively exploring the power of generative AI, I am writing in response to the 
National Science Foundation’s (NSF) Request for Information on the Development of 
an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan. At the Salon, we are committed to ensuring 
that artificial intelligence (AI) is developed and deployed in a way that promotes 
ethical integrity, social responsibility, and inclusive governance. AI has the 
transformative potential to drive positive change in the world, so we ask that you 
consider our recommendations to ensure that AI is guided by responsible principles 
and practices.  
Ensuring fairness, transparency, and societal good​
Among our core values, AI Salon’s members are invested in using AI for societal good. 
In December 2023, the Salon hosted #GPT4Good, a 24–hour collaboration that 
produced 150 custom chatbots for non-profit organizations.  
To that end, we advocate for AI systems free from harmful biases and designed to be 
transparent and accountable. AI should be developed with fairness in mind, ensuring 
that it benefits all people, regardless of background, identity, or circumstance. As the 
NSF and the Trump Administration consider AI regulation, we urge you to support 
policies that promote the use of AI for societal good—whether in healthcare, 
education, or environmental sustainability— that balance both holding bad actors 
accountable and encouraging innovation. 

Promoting a collaborative AI regulatory framework​
As mindful optimists, the Salon is invested in fostering an environment where AI can 
flourish safely. We support thoughtful regulation that promotes AI development and 
adoption by small enterprises and addresses AI risks. We urge the Administration to 
include small enterprises and diverse founders in all policy discussions to ensure 
guidelines that adequately promote responsible AI development and deployment 
across all players.  
Additionally, the Salon supports developing national standards that govern AI's 
ethical deployment. In 2024, over 700 AI bills were introduced in state legislatures, 
and 2025 is expected to supersede that number. These bills are rarely uniform in their 
definitions and requirements, creating a worrisome patchwork of complex and 
burdensome requirements. Our members’ innovative work is seldom limited to the 
boundaries of one state, and this patchwork of regulations would particularly affect 
small founders who do not have the financial and staffing resources to comply. To 
that end, we recommend that the Administration collaborate with the startup 
community and the public sector to harmonize national AI standards and develop 
safety practices.  
Protecting personal data and safeguarding security​
Data privacy and security are paramount in the age of AI. We advocate for policies 
that ensure AI systems handle personal data with the utmost care, with clear rules 
on data ownership and consent. Stronger protections are needed to guard against 
AI-driven cyberattacks and misinformation. We recommend that the Administration 
address these concerns through a national policy framework to help consumers 
better understand their rights and support comprehensive AI deployment.  
Balancing creativity and innovation​
As AI-generated content becomes more prevalent, we must address the ownership 
and copyright implications for creators and developers. We support fair intellectual 
property laws that balance the rights of traditional artists, content creators, and AI 
developers. Additionally, we advocate for updating patent laws to reflect the role of 
AI in innovation while ensuring that the process remains open and accessible to all. 
Preparing workers for an AI-driven future​
The rise of AI brings both opportunity and challenge. AI literacy is crucial for 
everyone—from policymakers to everyday citizens. We advocate for expanding AI 
education at all levels of society, from introductory courses to advanced training for 
professionals. Additionally, we believe that companies must take corporate 
responsibility for ensuring their employees understand AI's technical and ethical 
aspects, fostering a workforce that can make informed, ethical decisions. 

To ensure workers have the tools to succeed in new AI-enhanced roles, we urge the 
Administration to invest in reskilling initiatives, workforce transition plans, and 
educational programming to prepare students for future workforce needs.  
Enhancing democratic processes with AI tools​
We see AI as a powerful tool to improve governance. We support the use of 
AI-assisted governance to optimize policy design, resource allocation, and public 
health responses. However, this should be done transparently and in a way that 
promotes public participation. We recommend that the Administration study how AI 
can be used to enhance public consultation models, allowing citizens to engage 
meaningfully in policy development while safeguarding privacy and fairness. 
Greening AI for a sustainable future​
AI can contribute to and help mitigate the environmental impact of technological 
development. We recommend that the Administration support policies that address 
large AI models' carbon footprint and encourage energy-efficient AI development 
practices. Additionally, we support the use of AI in tackling climate change, from 
optimizing energy use to predicting and mitigating environmental risks, ensuring 
that AI becomes a tool for sustainability. 
Ensuring AI systems are safe and beneficial​
As AI becomes more complex and autonomous, we must ensure that it remains safe 
and aligned with human values. We advocate for policies that ensure robust AI 
design, preventing harmful behaviors and ensuring systems act as intended. We also 
support policies that promote human-AI collaboration, ensuring that AI augments 
human decision-making and does not replace it, fostering a future where AI 
enhances human capabilities rather than undermines them. 
Thank you for the opportunity to respond to this request for comments and we ask 
that you please consider our recommendations. We welcome the opportunity to 
further this conversation, so please feel free to reach out to Kathy Orellana at 
 if you have any questions.  
Sincerely,  
Daisy Thomas 
Leader, AI Salon Policy & Civic Engagement Guild

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”.
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial

I am an everyday American who owns a small illustration & design studio hich serves clients in the 
publishing industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my

The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to

back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make 
this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if 
a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be 
theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this 
way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the 
incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big 
Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of 
computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by 
Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing 
these things? 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday 
Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
•
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent,
so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. This must be an “opt-in”
system.  The “opt-out” approach suggested by some companies is inefficient and puts the onus on
creators to chase down every possible case of companies scraping their work.

•
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the
incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so
the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.
•
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring
them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or even anti-AI. I have long been what is called an “early adopter,” and many of 
my works have been created digitally.  But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of 
thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law. 
I’ve heard it asserted that AI is “essential to national security.”    While this is clearly a lie, I hope it does 
not become true.  Every LLM so far has proven to be rife with inaccuracies , false positives, false 
negatives, and what the tech sector calls “hallucinations.”  To base government actions in re national 
security on such unreliable systems would be disastrous. 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues. 
- Duncan Eagleson

Name: Anonymous Anonymous

General Comment
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”.
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my 
business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to 
destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create 
special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the 
work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI 
systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell 
it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to 
make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are 
suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly “fair 
use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the 
law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect 
the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big 
Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece 

of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by 
Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living 
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday 
Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:
•
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.
•
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the 
incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, 
so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.
•
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring 
them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI 
generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of 
hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

From, a concerned American 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial

I am an everyday American who believes strongly in the transformative power of art. As a visual 
artist and writer, I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build these 
skills into something I can proudly share with others, and have been lucky enough to be able to 
monetize this hobby – until recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to 
destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create 
special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other American and international creators is being taken 
and fed into these AI systems without our knowledge, consent, or any compensation. They 
ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us 
and cutting us out of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the 
incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday 
Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the 
incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, 
so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech. 
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them 
to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated. 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
Please remember that AI is not inevitable. By even choosing to call it “AI” we are giving the idea 
more credibility than it is worth. These machines and algorithms are just that, they are not 
sentient. They are not intelligent. They do not and can not think. They are gristle mills of stolen 
art of every single kind, churning out slop for the public on the very dark assumption that slop is 
all we want and, darker still, all we deserve.

General Comment
From:
Andi Santagata
Cartoonist
Upper Valley, Vermont
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am a working class American who has worked in the cartooning and video game industry for the past 17 years. I have worked hard for
years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been proud to contribute to the great American institutions of
entertainment that define us as a culture, from film to comic books.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American jobs and
bodies of work like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. Any work I create,
without my consent or knowledge, can be twisted to anyone else's use and profit. How would you feel if someone told you they could
take your entire life's work, act like they made it, and then sell it to other people without you seeing a dime?
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. I am here to say that the
American people are the backbone of American innovation.
The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things? Is it not incredibly un-American to say that anything you create is automatically free to use by the state or state-
approved corporations?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:

The government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our
work is used by AI systems. The AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what
material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. As someone with a robust history of work in game development, I've been proud to help develop
many AI systems of my own design, including pathing and modeling human behavior. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of
hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law - it would fundamentally destroy the
institution of American entertainment, one of our proudest accomplishments.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

March 14, 2025
From:
Rebecca Hayes
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American with a vested interest in the health of our creative industries and the negative 
effects that unchecked development of AI is likely to have on every industry.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and 
Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses with their 
recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the 
work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI 
systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it 
back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make 
this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if 
a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be 
theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this 
way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright 
law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big 
Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of 
computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by 

Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing 
these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators 
and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the
incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so
the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring
them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, 
and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of 
thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

General Comment
It is imperative that we do not allow AI engines to take advantage of loopholes in copyright law before it is too late. The AI systems made
by tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses with their recent

individual innovation and will also negatively impact the economy, as many of these creators rely on their work being marketable and will
not spend money they haven’t made.

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair

our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Timothy Block  
Email: 
General Comment
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just

Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

PUBLIC SUBMISSION
As of: March 21, 2025
Received: March 15, 2025
Status: 
Tracking No. m8b-02d3-tw5k
Comments Due: March 15, 2025
Submission Type: Web
Docket: NSF_FRDOC_0001
Recently Posted NSF Rules and Notices.

Request for Information: Development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan
Document: NSF_FRDOC_0001-DRAFT-6307
Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Anonymous Anonymous
General Comment
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their

training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

Kelsey Bratcher 
Logistics and Transportation Analyst 
Newport News, VA 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who supports small visual design businesses which serve clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the means to help this community flourish and those within the community to grow their skills and knowledge to
build their businesses, allowing them to earn a decent living and support their families – until recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threatens to destroy thousands of American small
businesses with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. The work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday
American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without consent or any compensation. They ingest the work, reassemble it,
and then sell it back to clients – directly competing with and cutting American artists out of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things? 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition: 
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems. 
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech. 
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated. 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law. 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

AI Letter

March 15, 2025
From:
Cas Hurst
Freelance Artist & Call Center Supervisor
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to 
build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family 
– until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:
●
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.
●
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech.
●
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.
